clue.text: Dance clubs serially introducing followers of Paddy Clarke?

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: each club letter introduces, coming just before, one laugh
serially means one after another, so a club goes before each laugh in turn

parts.note: Roddy Doyle's novel is Paddy Clarke Ha Ha Ha, so the words after the name are three has

explanation.surface: A dance club keeps bringing in fans of a Roddy Doyle novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy Clarke Ha Ha Ha is Roddy Doyle's Booker-winning novel, so the words that follow Paddy Clarke are HA HA HA; 'serially' puts a C (clubs) before each one.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin American ballroom dance with a quick triple step, named for its rhythm.

clue.text: Something Indian women wear during public holidays

indicators.note: the answer sits during, that is within, the run of letters in these two words

explanation.surface: A garment Indian women put on for festival days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' marks a hidden word: publiC HOLIdays. Holi, the Indian spring festival, is itself a public holiday, which helps the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A short, close-fitting blouse worn under a sari in India.

clue.text: Someone for young athletes to look up to? Mo's leaving town

indicators.note: Mo is leaving, so these two letters are taken out of the phrase

parts.words: Someone for young athletes to look up to
parts.note: a run model, read whimsically as a role model for runners
taken as the letters of the name, as in Mo Farah

explanation.surface: Mo Farah, a hero for young runners, quits a town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mo's' reads as Mo is: the athlete Mo Farah fits the running surface. Remove MO from A RUN MODEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Arundel is a small castle town in West Sussex, England.

clue.text: Water, perhaps, let me think it's deadly boring

parts.note: a water molecule has an oxygen atom between two hydrogens, written H-O-H
um is the noise of someone pausing to think

explanation.surface: A hesitant speaker muses that water is fatally dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' flags an unusual way to write water: not H2O but HOH, its atoms in the order they bond.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of weary indifference, so used for something tediously dull.

clue.text: Butler cracks enigmatic clue — so not hopeless!

indicators.note: Butler cracks the other letters, breaking in among them
an enigmatic clue is puzzling, so its letters are scrambled

parts.note: R. A. Butler, the British Conservative politician, was known as Rab

explanation.surface: A butler solves a baffling clue, so the solver's case isn't hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butler' is not a servant: Rab Butler was a senior British Conservative politician of the 1950s and 60s. The scrambled clue letters are broken open by his nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be cured or remedied is far from a lost cause.

clue.text: Net is cast in a suspicious part of a defensive system

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go in between the other pieces

parts.note: rum is an informal British word for odd or suspicious

indicators.note: the words are cast, thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A fishing net is thrown into a dodgy part of the defences.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum meaning odd or suspicious is informal British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A serum of antibodies is a component of the body's immune defences against disease.

clue.text: Poor clue's back to front

indicators.note: the back letter of the word for clue is moved to the front

parts.note: a hint is a clue

explanation.surface: A setter admits a clue is weak, its ending put first.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a full reversal: only the final T of HINT goes 'back to front'.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin excuse or argument is a weak, inadequate one.

clue.text: Rebellious set cuffing suspect seen to get nervous

indicators.note: the outer word cuffs the other, holding it like handcuffs
a rebel turns against authority, so this word is turned round

parts.note: to put something is to set it down

indicators.note: something suspect is not straight, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Unruly youths handcuffing a suspect who was spotted get jittery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rebellious' does double duty as a turning signal: a rebel turns against authority, so the word for set is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To tense up is to become stiff and anxious, a phrasal verb for growing nervous.

clue.text: Commonly used as Frankfurter dips?

definitions.meaning: a Frankfurter is a person from Frankfurt, which stands on the river Main, so their dip is a swim there

explanation.surface: Frankfurters are usually dunked in sauces.
explanation.walkthrough: The sausage is a red herring: a Frankfurter is a resident of Frankfurt am Main, bathing in its river.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means mostly or on the whole, and literally places a bather in the river Main.

clue.text: Refined tincture into which is dipped a second pen

indicators.note: the single letter is dipped into the run of the other letters

parts.note: couth means cultured or refined
or is the heraldic tincture gold

explanation.surface: A writer dips a pen into an elegant tincture.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, gold, is one of the heraldic tinctures, not an ink or medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-writer is a second author, pen being a metonym for writer.

clue.text: It could go off with a bang in Hollywood this evening

definitions.text: It could go off with a bang
definitions.meaning: a blasting explosive is something that detonates
the informal American spelling of the word for this evening

explanation.surface: Something explosive is happening in Hollywood tonight.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a trade name for a blasting explosive and also the US casual spelling of tonight.

clue.text: Chapel in Dumfriesshire bearing name of Roman city

indicators.note: the words are bearing the answer, carrying it within their letters

explanation.surface: A Scottish chapel carries the name of a Roman settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' marks a hidden word: chapeL IN DUMfriesshire. 'name of' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lindum Colonia was the Roman name for the settlement that became Lincoln.

clue.text: Out of true love, lady finally managed hugs

indicators.note: the outer word hugs the letters, holding them inside

parts.note: to boss is to manage or direct

indicators.note: finally picks the final letters of the two words before it

explanation.surface: Out of true love, a lady eventually managed some hugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of true love' looks like a phrase, but the definition stops at 'true'. 'finally' gives EY (from love and lady), which BOSSED 'hugs'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cross-eyed or squinting, so figuratively crooked or askew.

clue.text: "Pasta rings": line in new Alien

indicators.note: the single letter goes in the rearranged letters
a new version of the word, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A menu line advertising pasta hoops in a new Alien film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns ALIEN into ANELI, and L goes 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Small ring-shaped pasta, often used in soups, from the Italian for little rings.

clue.text: Tutee not excited about nucleus of charged or, possibly, uncharged particle

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go about the middle letter
excited letters are agitated into a fresh order
the nucleus is the central letter of the word

explanation.surface: A pupil unmoved by atomic physics wonders whether a particle is charged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges TUTEE NOT, which goes 'about' R, the centre of chaRged. 'or, possibly,' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypothetical neutral elementary particle, named like the neutrino, so it carries no charge.

clue.text: See 25
Regret turning over like one reaching North Pole, say

indicators.note: the word for regret is turned round

parts.note: to rue is to regret
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
from the saying 'like two peas in a pod', where each is one pea
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: An explorer regrets turning back before reaching the North Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North Pole' is split: North gives N and Pole, a person from Poland, is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pole is an inhabitant of Poland, an example of someone from the continent's nations.

clue.text: Allowed bill to add up, so this wine sent back

indicators.note: the whole sequence is sent back, read from the end

parts.note: let means allowed
AC, account, is a bill
to sum is to add up

explanation.surface: A diner lets the bill mount up, so sends the wine back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' reverses LET + AC + SUM; 'so this' points to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet wine made from muscat grapes.

clue.text: Great disappointment for ice cream lover? Topping embellishment

indicators.note: a cone with nothing in it, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: a cornet is an ice cream cone
O, nothing, is what a let-down leaves you with

explanation.surface: An ice cream fan is let down, yet a topping adds decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: An ice cream lover's worst let-down is a cornet with nothing in it, so O goes inside CORNET.
explanation.definitionFit: A small crown or ornamental band worn on top of the head.

clue.text: Queen's name included in list for Swampy?

indicators.note: the pieces are placed inside the word for list

parts.note: a ship lists when it leans
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Is the Queen's name on a list of environmental protesters like Swampy?
explanation.walkthrough: Swampy was a famous British road-protest campaigner of the 1990s, but here the word is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to Lerna, the marsh near Argos where the Hydra lived.

clue.text: The way to work round Emerald Isle sheep

indicators.note: the two letters go round the poetic name

parts.note: MO, modus operandi, is the way someone works
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland, the Emerald Isle

explanation.surface: A commuter route that skirts Ireland's sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed of sheep prized for its fine wool.

clue.text: Chap last in Tour: "I don't want any more cycling!"

indicators.note: the last letter of the word that follows
the letters are cycled, the first moving to the end

parts.note: Enough! is what someone says when they have had all they want

explanation.surface: A man at the end of the Tour de France says he has had enough of cycling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chap' is a verb, as cold air chaps skin. 'cycling' moves the E of ENOUGH to the end, giving OUGHEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold wind chaps the skin, making it cracked and coarse.

clue.text: Rabbit initially trapped by African, then catching a dim-witted friend of his

indicators.note: the assembled word then catches the next letter inside
the letter is trapped inside the word for an African

parts.note: a Berber is one of the native peoples of North Africa

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A rabbit is snared by an African who then grabs its slow friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his' refers back to Rabbit: the Uncle Remus character Brer Rabbit, whose foes include the dim Brer Bear.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Uncle Remus stories, the slow-witted bear is a companion of Brer Fox against Brer Rabbit.

clue.text: Loveless woman of some allure to set about Valentine's rival

indicators.note: the two letters are set about the rest
love is O, so the woman is without that letter

parts.note: a houri is a beautiful nymph of the Islamic paradise

explanation.surface: A loveless seductress is set to attack Valentine's love rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, as in tennis. In Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona, Valentine and Thurio both court Silvia.
explanation.definitionFit: The foolish suitor competing with Valentine for Silvia in Two Gentlemen of Verona.

clue.text: Personal training rep (very important person) killing Three Coins in a Fountain

indicators.note: killing removes those three letters wherever they occur

parts.note: PT stands for physical or personal training
taken as written
VIP stands for very important person
P, a penny, is a British coin, so three coins are three Ps

explanation.surface: A gym rep and a celebrity spoil the film Three Coins in the Fountain.
explanation.walkthrough: P is a penny, so 'killing Three Coins' removes three Ps from PTREPVIP. The film Three Coins in the Fountain is set at this Roman fountain.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Baroque fountain in Rome into which tourists throw coins.

clue.text: I'd find out which items are odd, perhaps even

indicators.note: only the odd-numbered letters of the phrase are taken: first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: Someone will find out which things are odd, or even.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd/even puzzle misleads: 'which items are odd' picks the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of I'D FIND OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Used to suggest a stronger possibility, as in many if not all, meaning possibly even.

clue.text: Strong liquor street bar had in short supply

indicators.note: the word is cut short, its last letter dropped

parts.note: an ingot is a bar of metal

explanation.surface: A bar on the street had little strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' tempts you to a pub, but it is a metal ingot, shortened to INGO.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for strong ale or beer.

clue.text: A prominent hole — the suspect …

indicators.note: suspect letters are not to be trusted in their order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A conspicuous gap, and the suspect...
explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: the whole clue rearranges into the phrase it describes. The ellipsis runs on into 26 Across, which answers it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for an obvious problem that everyone avoids, like a glaring hole.

clue.text: … how should we respond? Not at all

definitions.meaning: a reply to the obvious problem in the preceding clue: say nothing about it
the polite reply to being thanked

explanation.surface: How should we react to the awkward subject? Not at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to 25/14: the polite advice for an obvious problem everyone ignores is to keep quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase both advises silence and is a stock reply, like no problem, to thanks.

clue.text: See 26
